term: "Model Monitoring"

## Simple explanation

Model monitoring means checking a deployed AI system over time to see whether
it remains healthy and useful. Teams track system behavior as well as model
quality, because either can degrade.

## Technical explanation

Monitoring may include service metrics such as latency and errors, input and
output statistics, data-quality checks, drift indicators, and outcome metrics
when ground-truth labels become available. Monitoring signals are proxies:
they can identify changes but do not always prove that model quality has
changed.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Production data, user behavior, dependencies, and traffic patterns can change
after a model is evaluated. Monitoring helps teams detect incidents, decide
when investigation or retraining is needed, and verify the impact of a
deployment.

## How it works

Instrument the serving pipeline, define expected ranges or alert conditions,
and retain enough information to diagnose issues while respecting privacy and
retention policies. Compare current data with suitable baselines. When labels
are delayed, use proxy signals cautiously and confirm suspected problems with
direct evaluation where possible.

## Practical example

A deployed text classifier records request latency, prediction rates, and
input validation failures. When the share of a certain class changes
unexpectedly, the team investigates whether traffic or the underlying data
has shifted before deciding to retrain.

## Common misconceptions

- Monitoring input drift alone does not establish that predictive performance has degraded.
- Alerts need owners and response procedures; dashboards alone do not resolve incidents.
- Retraining should follow evidence and evaluation, not every detected distribution change.
